nameStory: Cylindrocystis brebissonii doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists stick with its scientific name that describes its shape. The name 'Cylindrocystis' comes from Greek words meaning 'cylinder' and 'bladder,' perfectly describing these tiny, tube-shaped single-celled algae. It's named after French botanist Alphonse de Brébisson, who was a master at studying microscopic algae in the 1800s.
description: **Note: This identification requires a microscope** Cylindrocystis brebissonii is a single-celled freshwater alga that you'll never see with the naked eye - each cell is only about 0.01-0.03 millimeters long! Under a microscope, it looks like a tiny green cylinder or sausage shape. These microscopic plants live in acidic waters like bogs and help form the green films you might notice on pond surfaces, though you'd need magnification to see the individual cells that make up those films.

idTips.label: Cell Shape
idTips.description: Cylindrical cells that are 2-4 times longer than they are wide, like tiny green hot dogs under the microscope

idTips.label: Chloroplast Pattern
idTips.description: Two star-shaped green chloroplasts (the parts that make food from sunlight) positioned at each end of the cell

idTips.label: Cell Wall
idTips.description: Smooth, clear cell wall without any bumps, ridges, or decorative patterns that some similar algae have

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Cells measure 8-25 micrometers wide and 15-50 micrometers long (much smaller than the width of human hair)

habitat: Found in acidic, nutrient-poor waters throughout New England, especially in sphagnum bogs, acidic ponds, and slow-moving streams. Look for it in the quiet backwaters of mountain streams or in boggy areas where blueberries and pitcher plants grow. It prefers soft water with low mineral content, often mixed with other microscopic algae in the greenish films on water surfaces.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm up in late spring, reproducing and forming visible green films on pond surfaces that hint at their microscopic presence below.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when populations can bloom in suitable acidic waters, contributing to the green tinge in bog pools and quiet stream edges.
seasonality.fall: Still present but less active as temperatures drop, often persisting in protected bog pools even as surface ice begins to form.
seasonality.winter: Survives under ice in a dormant state, waiting for spring warmth to resume active growth and reproduction.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these tiny algae are actually helping to terraform our planet the same way they have for over a billion years - they're direct descendants of the ancient algae that first pumped oxygen into Earth's atmosphere, making complex life possible!
confusionNotes: Under the microscope, it's easily confused with other cylindrical algae like Netrium species, but Cylindrocystis has those distinctive star-shaped chloroplasts at each end rather than a single central chloroplast. Remember: 'Cylindrocystis has chloroplasts at the tips like green stars on cylinder ends.'
contextualKnowledge: This species represents one of the simpler forms of plant life - it's neither a true plant nor exactly what we think of as seaweed, but rather belongs to a group called charophyte algae that are considered the ancestors of all land plants. Finding it requires serious magnification, so it's mainly of interest to naturalists with microscopes or those taking water quality samples.
compareHints: **Note: Identification uncertainty flagged** Cylindrocystis brebissonii is the only commonly reported Cylindrocystis species in New England. It differs from related algae in the same family by having a simpler, cylindrical shape rather than the half-moon or crescent shapes of desmids, and lacks the constricted middle that many similar single-celled algae display. Its star-shaped chloroplasts at each cell end are a key distinguishing feature from other cylindrical algae.
